Lab 019 · Lessons 019–020 · simulation using the lesson's numbers

Tuning Lab

Mia tunes the Feeding Frenzy on Reef 2. Change the gull's dive speed and the sardine's bite window, then get the change into the game three ways and watch the hours add up. Break the data, guard it, and bake it for the phone. Then (Lesson 020) move the gulls' steal rule into a hot-reloaded script, fix its traps and pay its speed bill.

Mia needs about 120 tweaks for one level. Goal: live tuning that reaches every fish, a validator that stops bad data, and baked data the phone loads in under 100 ms.

Lesson 019: data-driven design

      
    
    
    
    
    
      
    Lesson 020: scripting and hot reload
    
      
      
    
      
  
      

  
      
    
      What this shows
      
    
      
      
      Code says how, data says how much
      With numbers in code, each tweak waits for a programmer and a compile: 899 s. In data files it's 100 s; reloaded live, 15 s. 120 tweaks drop from 30 hours to 30 minutes.
      
      
      Read, don't copy; check everything
      A value copied at spawn never sees a live change. Data with no schema breaks quietly: one extra "e" stops every gull diving. A validator and stable IDs catch all three mistakes on save.
      
      
      Text for people, binary for the phone
      Parsing 3.2 MB of JSON costs 1,900 ms and 41 MB of garbage at start-up. A bake step makes one 0.6 MB file that loads in 40 ms. Typed structs cut tuning reads from 0.27 ms to 0.006 ms a tick.
      
    
      
    
      
      
      Engine in C#, rules in scripts
      A rule in C# costs 899 s a try: 10 hours for Mia's 40 tries. A Lua script with hot reload costs 15 s: 10 minutes. The script sees only a 14-function API.
      
      
      Reloading code keeps old things alive
      State kept in the script resets on every save (50 s before a steal). A script that subscribes itself leaves old versions running. State goes in components; the engine keeps rules by name; every call is guarded.
      
      
      C# loops, the script decides
      Each crossing into Lua costs about 1.2 µs. One call per gull: 4.2 ms a frame and 128 KB of garbage. One batched call for the 60 gulls near a carrier: 0.12 ms, inside the 1 ms budget.
      
    
      
    
      This lab is a simulation, not a measurement. The times are the lesson's numbers: 720 s waiting for a programmer, 60 s to edit, 29 s to compile the Simulation (Lesson 018), 90 s to play back to the Frenzy, 10 s to edit a file and 5 s to see a live change. The phone numbers are the lesson's approximate profiler capture. The reef animation only shows the effect of each value; it is not Sky Hopper's real simulation. The steal-rule panel (Lesson 020) uses the lesson's approximate numbers: 1.2 µs per crossing into Lua, 0.9 µs per rule, 50 ns for the same rule in C#, 4 ms to compile a script, and hunger growing 0.012 a second. No Lua runs on this page.
